difficultyReason: The argument rests on a hidden methodological assumption: that the comparison group is equivalent in all relevant respects. The correct weakener attacks that buried premise rather than the surface causal claim. Distractors include a strengthener, an out-of-scope comparative, a choice that attacks a peripheral premise without touching the conclusion, and a plausible-sounding but irrelevant fact.
stimulus: A pharmaceutical researcher reported that patients who received a new antibiotic for bacterial pneumonia recovered an average of three days faster than patients who received the standard treatment during the same period at the same hospital. The researcher concluded that the new antibiotic is more effective than the standard treatment for bacterial pneumonia.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researcher's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients assigned to the new antibiotic had, on average, significantly milder cases of bacterial pneumonia at the time of admission than those assigned to the standard treatment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The standard treatment has been used successfully for bacterial pneumonia for more than two decades.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The new antibiotic costs substantially more per treatment course than the standard treatment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several patients in the standard treatment group experienced minor side effects that did not affect their rate of recovery.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The hospital at which the study was conducted sees a higher volume of pneumonia cases than most hospitals in the region.

explanations.correct: The researcher assumes the two patient groups were comparable at baseline. If new-antibiotic patients had milder cases to begin with, the faster recovery could reflect disease severity rather than drug efficacy — a classic confound that severs the causal link between treatment and outcome.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a confounding variable (baseline disease severity) that provides an alternative explanation for the faster recovery, directly undermining the conclusion that the new antibiotic is more effective.
explanations.B: Opposite-answer trap. Establishing the standard treatment's long track record slightly bolsters its credibility, which if anything weakens the case for switching — but this does not undermine the researcher's specific comparative-efficacy conclusion.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. Cost is irrelevant to whether the new antibiotic is medically more effective; the conclusion is about efficacy, not value or prescribing policy.
explanations.D: Too narrow / attacks peripheral premise. Minor side effects that did not affect recovery rates have no bearing on the comparative recovery-speed finding that grounds the conclusion.
explanations.E: Irrelevant. Hospital case volume says nothing about whether the new antibiotic outperforms the standard treatment within that hospital's comparison.

difficultyReason: The argument is a multi-step predictive chain (policy → behavioral change → economic outcome). The correct answer attacks the second link — the move from behavioral change to economic outcome — which students often overlook because the first link seems like the obvious target. Distractors include a strengthener, a choice that attacks the first link only, an irrelevant statistic, and a subject-shift trap.
stimulus: A city council economist argued as follows: by eliminating the downtown parking subsidy, the city will force commuters to seek cheaper alternatives such as public transit. Because commuters who switch to public transit will no longer spend money at downtown parking garages, the revenue currently collected by those private garages will decline sharply, causing several garages to close. Therefore, eliminating the parking subsidy will ultimately reduce the total number of parking spaces available downtown.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Many commuters who currently use the subsidized parking would continue to drive downtown even if the subsidy were eliminated, because no public transit route serves their neighborhoods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Private parking garages in cities that eliminated similar subsidies typically converted their facilities into mixed-use commercial space rather than closing them entirely.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The city's public transit system has sufficient unused capacity to accommodate a large influx of new riders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parking garage operators in the downtown area have consistently opposed the parking subsidy since it was introduced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Eliminating the parking subsidy would reduce the city's annual budget expenditure by several million dollars.

explanations.correct: The economist's conclusion depends on the chain: subsidy removal → commuters switch to transit → garages lose revenue → garages close → fewer total spaces. Choice B cuts the final link: if garages convert to commercial space rather than close, they would no longer provide parking spaces regardless — or more precisely, the spaces are lost through conversion, not closure driven by revenue decline. More importantly, it shows the garages would not simply 'close' and be replaced by nothing; they'd repurpose, meaning the causal mechanism for space reduction is broken. The real-world comparator undermines the specific prediction that the revenue decline causes closures that reduce spaces.
explanations.A: Too narrow / attacks the first link only. If many commuters keep driving, garages may not lose as much revenue — but this only weakens the premise that commuters will switch; it does not address what happens to garages if some do switch. The conclusion could still follow from a partial shift, so this choice leaves the conclusion largely intact.
explanations.B: Correct. Attacks the critical second-to-final link by showing that even if garages lose revenue, the predicted outcome (reduction in total spaces) does not follow — garages convert rather than close, and conversions remove spaces through a mechanism independent of the economist's causal chain.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. If transit has spare capacity, the shift away from driving is more feasible, which supports the economist's predicted behavioral change and thus bolsters, rather than weakens, the argument.
explanations.D: Irrelevant. Garage operators' political stance on the subsidy has no logical bearing on whether eliminating it will reduce available parking spaces.
explanations.E: Subject shift. Budget savings are a separate consequence of the policy; whether the city saves money does not bear on whether total downtown parking spaces will decrease.

difficultyReason: The stimulus involves a methodological argument about linguistic evidence: a hidden assumption that written records are a reliable proxy for spoken language change. The correct weakener attacks that unstated methodological premise, which students must first identify. Distractors include a strengthener, a reversed-causation misapplication, a peripheral-premise attacker, and an out-of-scope comparison.
stimulus: Historians of language have long debated when the Latin spoken in the western Roman provinces began diverging into the distinct precursors of modern Romance languages. A historical linguist recently argued that this divergence began no earlier than the sixth century CE, citing evidence that written documents from the fifth century across different provinces show remarkably uniform Latin grammar and vocabulary.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the historical linguist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Many fifth-century Latin documents were produced by a small class of highly educated scribes who were trained to write in a standardized classical Latin that differed markedly from the spoken vernacular of ordinary people.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sixth-century documents from different provinces show considerably greater variation in Latin grammar and vocabulary than fifth-century documents do.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Modern Romance languages differ from one another in phonology more than in grammatical structure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historians have recovered relatively fewer written documents from the fifth century than from the sixth century.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some linguists believe that the divergence of Romance languages was accelerated by the migration of Germanic peoples into western Roman territories.

explanations.correct: The linguist infers that uniformity in written documents reflects uniformity in spoken language, and therefore concludes that spoken divergence had not yet begun. Choice A exposes the fatal flaw in this inference: written Latin was a standardized prestige register maintained by trained scribes, not a faithful record of vernacular speech. Uniformity in documents could coexist with substantial spoken divergence already underway, directly undermining the evidentiary basis of the sixth-century dating.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the hidden methodological premise — that written uniformity tracks spoken uniformity — by providing a mechanism (scribal standardization) that would produce uniform documents even if spoken dialects were already diverging.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. If sixth-century documents show greater variation, this is consistent with the linguist's claim that divergence became apparent from the sixth century onward; it actually supports rather than undermines the argument.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. Whether Romance languages differ more in phonology than grammar is irrelevant to when divergence of the spoken precursors began; it concerns the endpoint of divergence, not the starting point the linguist is dating.
explanations.D: Peripheral-premise attacker. Fewer fifth-century documents might raise questions about sample size, but the argument does not hinge on document quantity — it hinges on uniformity among the documents that do exist. This choice marginally complicates the evidence base without touching the core inference from written to spoken uniformity.
explanations.E: Subject shift. The claim about Germanic migration may relate to what accelerated divergence, but the linguist's conclusion concerns when divergence began, not what caused its acceleration. This choice neither attacks nor supports the sixth-century start date.
